title: Impulse and force–time graphs; Electric charge and charging; Charge and current
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: F01-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; F01-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; D10-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; D10-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: D10-1#N.4a, EL01-1#N.3, F01-1#N.2, D10-1#N.12, EL01-1#N.6a, F01-1#N.4a, EL01-1#N.11, EL01-1#N.12.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Neutron
items.clue: Particle that carries no charge at all.

items.label: Electron
items.clue: Negative particle that an object gains or loses to become charged.

items.label: Crumple zone
items.clue: Car feature that lengthens the stopping time, making the average force smaller.

items.label: Impulse
items.clue: Vector in N s pointing along the resultant force, not necessarily along the motion.

questions.stem: A sledge on level snow is pulled horizontally with a constant force of 60.0 N for 4.00 s. Throughout this time it slides forwards and the frictional force on it is 22.0 N. What is the magnitude of the impulse delivered to the sledge by the resultant force during the 4.00 s?

options.text: 240 N s
328 N s
9.5 N s
152 N s

questions.explanation: Resultant force = 60.0 − 22.0 = 38.0 N. J = FΔt = 38.0 × 4.00 = 152 N s, forwards.

questions.stem: In an electron beam in a vacuum tube, 1.5 × 10¹⁵ electrons pass through a cross-section of the beam in 8.0 s at a steady rate. What is the magnitude of the current in the beam? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
A small plastic bead has a net charge of −4.8 × 10⁻¹⁷ C. Which statement correctly describes the bead? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

options.text: It has 3.0 × 10² fewer electrons than protons.
It has 3.0 × 10² more electrons than protons.
It has 3.0 × 10² electrons and no protons at all.
It has 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁷ more electrons than protons.

questions.stem: Two identical 0.50 kg gliders on an air track each move at 2.0 m s⁻¹ towards an obstacle. Glider 1 hits a steel buffer and bounces straight back at 2.0 m s⁻¹; the contact lasts 0.010 s. Glider 2 hits a foam pad and stops; the contact lasts 0.040 s. How many times larger is the average force on glider 1 than the average force on glider 2?

options.text: 1, as both gliders arrive with the same speed

questions.stem: Predict first. A copper wire forms part of a circuit carrying a steady direct current. Which statement about the charge carriers in the wire is correct?

options.text: Free electrons drift slowly towards the positive terminal of the cell.
Electrons travel at close to the speed of light, so a lamp lights at the instant the switch closes.
Protons move along the wire, from the positive terminal towards the negative one.
Electrons leave the cell and some are used up in the lamp, so fewer return to the cell.

questions.explanation: In a metal the charge carriers are free electrons. Being negative, they are attracted towards the positive terminal, and on average they drift only slowly (typically well under 1 mm s⁻¹).

questions.stem: In an experiment, the charges on four oil drops were measured in arbitrary units as 4.2, 7.0, 9.8 and 15.4 units. Assuming that charge is quantised, what is the largest value of the basic unit of charge that is consistent with all four results?

options.text: 2.8 units
0.70 units
4.2 units
1.4 units

questions.explanation: 4.2, 7.0, 9.8 and 15.4 are 3, 5, 7 and 11 times 1.4. No larger value divides all four exactly.

questions.stem: Several wires meet at a junction in a circuit with steady currents. A student measures a current of 1.20 A in one wire leading into the junction, and currents of 0.70 A and 0.40 A in two wires leading out of it. The ammeters are ideal and read correctly. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The other wires at the junction carry a net current of 0.10 A away from it.
0.10 A of the current was used up as charge passed through the junction.
Charge is building up at the junction at a rate of 0.10 C each second.
An unmeasured wire must carry 2.30 A, the sum of the three measured currents.

questions.stem: A copper wire has a thick section X joined to a thin section Y, and there is a steady current in the wire. How do the currents I_X and I_Y in the two sections compare?

options.text: They are equal: the same charge passes each cross-section per second.
I_Y is greater, since the charges move faster through the narrow section Y.
I_X is greater, since the thick section X holds more of the charge carriers.
It depends on the direction of the current, as current decreases along a wire.
